A.explanation: This is $480 \times 2/3$. It inverts the orders, using $2 \times 480 = 3 \times \lambda$ instead of $3 \times 480 = 2 \times \lambda$.

C.explanation: This is $480 \times 2$. It doubles the blue wavelength but ignores the given third-order and second-order numbers.

D.explanation: This is $480 \times 3$. It multiplies by the blue order only and omits division by the unknown order 2.

hints: Notice the same grating spacing $d$ and the same angle $\theta$ are used for the $n=3$ blue maximum at $480 \text{ nm}$ and the $n=2$ unknown maximum.
Recall the grating equation $d \sin\theta = n\lambda$, so for fixed $d \sin\theta$ the product $n\lambda$ must be equal for the two overlapping maxima.
Set $3 \times 480 \text{ nm}$ equal to $2 \times \lambda_{unknown}$ and solve for $\lambda_{unknown}$.
walkthrough: Identify the common condition: both beams use the same grating and diffract to the same angle $\theta$, so $d \sin\theta$ is identical for the two maxima.
State the grating rule for normal incidence: $d \sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $n$ is the order number.
Apply it to each light: $d \sin\theta = 3 \times 480 \text{ nm}$ for blue light and $d \sin\theta = 2 \times \lambda_{unknown}$ for the unknown light.
Equate the right-hand sides because the left-hand sides are equal: $2\lambda_{unknown} = 3 \times 480 \text{ nm}$.
Calculate: $\lambda_{unknown} = 1440/2 \text{ nm} = 720 \text{ nm}$, with the same wavelength unit. This is option B.
